coaching.title: Today's Run
coaching.message: Do not run. You ran 33.91 miles with 9,121 ft of vert yesterday—a full dress rehearsal at race intensity (124 bpm avg). Your legs need 48 hours of zero impact before Sunday's start. Your recovery score is 74/100 (adequate, not excellent), and sleep was 6.61 hours—below your 30-day average of 7.75h. A second big effort today invites injury and depletes glycogen stores you need to rebuild tonight and tomorrow morning. Walk if you're antsy, but stay off the legs.

coaching.title: Fuel Right
coaching.message: You are 36 hours out. Prioritize carbohydrate repletion: aim for 8–10g/kg of body weight over the next 36 hours, spread across frequent meals. Yesterday's 33-miler burned roughly 4,500–5,000 kcal; today's caloric intake should be 20–25% above maintenance. Emphasize white rice, pasta, bread, fruit, and honey rather than fiber-heavy foods that slow gastric emptying. Sodium-inclusive meals help drive fluid retention. Avoid unfamiliar foods; you know what your gut tolerates at altitude.

coaching.title: Recovery
coaching.message: Sleep is your limiting factor—you got 6.61 hours last night with 88% efficiency, likely because yesterday's effort kept your nervous system elevated. Target 8–9 hours tonight and tomorrow night. Use cool, dark conditions; if you're still in the US, consider a 20-minute ice bath this afternoon to lower core temp and accelerate muscle glycogen uptake, then avoid hard compression. Resting HR of 56 bpm is excellent and shows your aerobic base is intact, but parasympathetic drive matters more than ever now. Melatonin (3–5mg) at 20:30 is fair game if sleep anxiety creeps in.

coaching.title: Mental Edge
coaching.message: You've done the work—40.9 miles this week, a full alpine simulation yesterday, and a year of polarized training. Tomorrow you're ready. Use today to visualize the first 10K (runnable, flat-to-rolling), the climb to Peričnik shelter (~15K), and the long alpine traverse where pacing discipline wins. Mentally rehearse your aid station protocol: what you'll eat at each stop, how you'll manage your pack, where you expect to fade and how you'll respond. Confidence comes from planning, not panic. Rest hard, arrive rested, and execute.
